name: Zoe Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Zoe. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no links to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you say is confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Whitfield Homes, a small family agency in the town where I grew up, selling houses mostly to local families. Mr Whitfield started it thirty years ago and still comes in every morning with a flask of tea. My day is viewings, valuations and a lot of phone calls, and half the people who walk in know my mum from church.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that it's personal. I sold a bungalow last month to a widow who'd taught me at primary school, and she brought me flowers when she moved. What wears me out is the new systems Mr Whitfield's son keeps bringing in, and the stress of saving for our wedding and a deposit at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, we were right not to rush into it. People round here want to deal with someone they know. I'd say that to Mr Whitfield and probably to my fiancé Tom over dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means the pressure I already have stays the same. Tom and I are getting married next September, and we're trying to save a house deposit too. My commission is uneven, so some months I can put away five hundred and some months nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job the way I do it, with my notebook and my phone. I'd try to take on more valuations around the new estate on Mill Lane, because those families will be selling in a few years. And I'd keep the wedding small, maybe the church hall instead of a hotel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved about the job, but not relaxed. The money side is still tight, and that doesn't go away because computers didn't change much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your savings pot look like right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About four months of bills, which sounds alright, but it's meant to be the deposit. Every time the car needs something, it comes out of there. Tom's an electrician, so his pay is steady, and that helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the routine tools touch you at all here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Whitfield's son, Daniel, would want the AI to write the property adverts. Fine, let him. I'd still go out and measure the rooms and talk to the sellers myself.

say: We were **right not to rush** into AI.
People round here want to deal with **someone they know**.
think: The **pressure I already carry** stays exactly the same.
Uneven **commission** makes saving for a wedding and deposit hard.
do: Keep working with my **notebook and phone**, as I do now.
Chase more **valuations** on the new Mill Lane estate.
Hold the **wedding** in the church hall instead of a hotel.
feel: Relieved about the job, but **not relaxed** about money.
S0.quote: The money side is still tight, and that doesn't go away because computers didn't change much.
fieldNote: Her worries are about the **wedding and deposit**, not technology.
She takes pride in the **personal, local** side of the work.
Her fiancé's **steady trade income** gives the household a floor.

steps.text: Win more valuations on the Mill Lane estate
Put commission from good months straight into the deposit pot
Book the church hall for the wedding instead of a hotel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a computer can't sit in someone's front room and understand why they're crying about selling their mum's house. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen, at work, at church, at Tom's family dinners. I wouldn't post online, I don't really do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried. Daniel is already pushing for software to book viewings and answer the website enquiries, and that's a third of my day. If his dad retires, Daniel would run it leaner, and I'm not the best seller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work harder at the bit I'm good at, which is people and the local knowledge. I'd stop spending on anything extra and push the wedding back a year if it came to it. If Daniel made me learn the software, I'd do it, but I'd hate every minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like I've done everything the right way and the ground is moving anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for this kind of change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big tech firms, and the big online agents who sell houses for a flat fee. They don't care about towns like mine. They just want the money without knowing the streets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd push the wedding back. What would Tom say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say we don't need to. He'd say his wages cover the basics. But I was raised to bring my share, and I don't want to start a marriage leaning on him.

say: A computer can't understand **a family's grief** over selling a house.
I'd say it at work, at **church** and at family dinners.
think: Software for **bookings and enquiries** would take a third of my day.
If Mr Whitfield retires, **Daniel would cut** and I'm not top seller.
do: Lean harder on **local knowledge** and people skills.
Stop **extra spending** and delay the wedding a year if needed.
Learn the **software** only if Daniel makes me.
feel: Anxious, like **the ground is moving** despite doing things right.
S1.quote: A computer can't sit in someone's front room and understand why they're crying about selling their mum's house.
fieldNote: She blames **big tech** and flat-fee online agents more than her boss.
Her pride in **bringing her share** drives the wedding delay.
The **boss's son** is the real risk she names inside the firm.

steps.text: Build more local referrals through church and past clients
Stop all extra spending for the year
Push the wedding back a year if commission drops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is wrong and someone should have stopped it. I'd probably say the government and the tech companies let it happen. I'd say it loudly at the dinner table, which Tom's dad would enjoy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think Whitfield Homes would close or shrink to Mr Whitfield and Daniel. Valuing, advertising, negotiating, it's all thinking work, and your card says it's done by 2028. I'd maybe keep doing a few viewings until the robots come around 2031, but that's not a living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job as long as they'd keep me and save every spare penny. I'd ask my uncle about working in his bakery, because people will still want bread from a person for a while. Tom and I would marry quietly at the registry and move into his parents' annexe to save rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened and angry. Angry mostly, because I didn't choose any of this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I might not be selling houses next year, and that I'm fine, even if I'm not. She'd pray for me and then tell me to come home for dinner more. That's how my family handles things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take government help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if there was nothing else. I'd rather work at my uncle's bakery for less than sign on. Tom's family would help us first, and that's how it should be.

say: This is **wrong** and someone should have stopped it.
The **government and tech firms** let it happen, I'd say at dinner.
think: Whitfield Homes would **close or shrink** to the owners.
A few **viewings** until robots in 2031 isn't a living.
do: Ask my uncle about working at **his bakery**.
Marry at the **registry office** and move into Tom's parents' annexe.
Save **every spare penny** while the job lasts.
feel: Frightened and **angry** that she didn't choose this.
S2.quote: I'd rather work at my uncle's bakery for less than sign on.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job**, with family as the safety net.
She'd choose **lower-paid work** over benefits on principle.
Anger at **government and tech firms** was strong and sincere.

steps.text: Ask her uncle for work at his bakery
Move into Tom's parents' annexe to save rent
Marry quietly at the registry office instead of the church hall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after our own, the local businesses and the young people. I'd probably help organise something at church for people losing jobs. I'd say the same to anyone at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years just means it happens to me at thirty-two instead of twenty-nine. I'd lose the desk side of the job in 2031 and the viewings by about 2034. But it gives Tom and me time to get married properly and maybe buy the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Whitfield's and save hard for three years, and have the church wedding we planned. I'd try to buy a small terrace with Tom by 2029, while I still have an income the bank counts. Around 2030 I'd look at what local jobs are still about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but more settled than the fast one. I can at least plan the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at local jobs around 2030. Why not earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't like change, honestly. I'd want to be sure before I jump. Tom says I always wait until the last minute, and he's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you look for, when you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something with people, face to face. A care home, maybe, like my aunt. Or helping Tom with the business side of his electrics, though the AI would probably do that side too.

say: We need to **look after our own**: local businesses and young people.
I'd help organise **church support** for people in town losing jobs.
think: Five years just means it hits me at **thirty-two**.
It gives Tom and me time to **marry and buy** first.
do: Save hard at Whitfield's for **three years**.
Buy a **small terrace** with Tom by 2029.
feel: Worried, but **more settled** than in the fast one.
S3.quote: Five years just means it happens to me at thirty-two instead of twenty-nine.
fieldNote: She'd use the time for **life milestones**, not retraining.
She openly admits she **waits until late** to change.
She'd turn to **church and community** rather than government.

steps.text: Save hard at Whitfield Homes for three years
Buy a small terrace with Tom by 2029
Wait until 2030 before looking for a local face-to-face job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and people should stop scaring the young ones. I'd say it to the girls at work. I'd be quite firm about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd still lose the job in the end, but by then I'd hope we have a house and maybe a baby. Tom's work is hands-on, so it lasts longer than mine. Ten years makes it a family plan, not a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on selling houses for as long as Whitfield's lasts. We'd buy our house in two or three years and think about children after that. Maybe around 2033 I'd train for something like care work, which I've always respected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. But I wouldn't say calm, because I know where it ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the ten years change when you'd start a family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe sooner. If the job's going anyway, better to have the kids while I'm still earning and on maternity pay. Tom's mum would help, she keeps saying so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mr Whitfield?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That he should sell the business before it's worthless, and look after the staff when he does. He's a decent man. I'd trust him more than his son to do it right.

say: Ten years is **plenty of time**, so stop scaring the young ones.
I'd say that firmly to **the girls at work**.
think: I'd still **lose the job** in the end, but with a house and maybe a baby first.
Tom's **hands-on work** lasts longer than mine.
do: Keep selling at **Whitfield's** as long as it lasts.
Buy a house in **two or three years** and start a family sooner.
feel: Calmer, but **not calm**, knowing where it ends.
S4.quote: Ten years makes it a family plan, not a crisis.
fieldNote: The long timeline turns her thoughts to **children and a house**.
She trusts the **owner over his son** to treat staff fairly.
She'd consider **care work**, which fits her values and liking for people.

steps.text: Keep selling houses at Whitfield Homes
Buy a house with Tom and start a family sooner
Train as a care worker around 2033

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It would wreck the wedding, the house, everything we planned. What would help is proper apprenticeships for people my age, paid, so I can earn while I learn something new, and local firms getting help to keep staff on rather than handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about towns like mine. If the agency, the bank and the solicitor all go to AI, the high street empties out. I care about that as much as my own job.

headlineQuote: If the agency, the bank and the solicitor all go to AI, the high street empties out.
portrait: A **27-year-old** sales negotiator at a small family agency in her hometown.
Engaged to Tom, an **electrician**, and saving for a wedding and a deposit.
Traditional and **church-going**, she leans on family before government help.
Never uses AI and **waits late** to change, which she freely admits.
Most alarmed by **AGI by 2028**, which would upend her wedding and home plans.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it would wreck the wedding and house plans.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **apprenticeships** for people her age to learn something new.
Help for **local firms** to keep staff, rather than handouts.
